Generalizations of the Image Conjecture and the Mathieu ConjectureThanks: The author has been partially supported by NSA Grant R1-07-0053

Wenhua Zhao
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We first propose a generalization of the image conjecture [Z3] for the commuting differential operators related with classical orthogonal polynomials. We then show that the non-trivial case of this generalized image conjecture is equivalent to a variation of the Mathieu conjecture [Ma] from integrals of GG-finite functions over reductive Lie groups GG to integrals of polynomials over open subsets of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with any positive measures. Via this equivalence, the generalized image conjecture can also be viewed as a natural variation of Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem [DK] on Laurent polynomials with no constant terms. To put all the conjectures above in a common setting, we introduce what we call the Mathieu subspaces of associative algebras. We also discuss some examples of Mathieu subspaces from other sources and derive some general results on this newly-introduced notion.

Key words and phrases: 
Orthogonal polynomials, commuting differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients, the image conjecture, the Mathieu conjecture, Mathieu subspaces, the polynomial moment problem
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
33C45, 32W99, 14R15

1. Introduction

1.1. Background and Motivation

The main motivations and contents of this paper are as follows.

First, in [Z3] a so-called image conjecture (IC) on images of commuting differential operators of polynomial algebras of order one with constant leading coefficients has been proposed. It has also been shown there that the well-known Jacobian conjecture proposed by O. H. Keller [Ke] (See also [BCW] and [E]) and, more generally, the vanishing conjecture [Z1], [Z2] on differential operators (of any order) with constant coefficients, are actually equivalent to some special cases of the IC.

Second, as pointed out in [Z2], all classical orthogonal polynomials in one or more variables can be obtained from some commuting differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients. Unfortunately, most of these differential operators are not differential operators of polynomial algebras. Instead, they are differential operators of some localizations of polynomial algebras such as Laurent polynomial algebras, etc.

Note that, due to their applications in many different areas of mathematics such as in ODE, PDE, the eigenfunction problems and representation theory, orthogonal polynomials have been under intense study by mathematicians in the last two centuries. For example, in [SHW] published in 19401940, about 20002000 published articles on orthogonal polynomials mostly in one variable had been included. Therefore it will also be interesting to consider the IC for the commuting differential operators related with classical orthogonal polynomials.

Unfortunately, the straightforward generalization of the IC from polynomial algebras to their localizations does not hold in general. In this paper, we propose another generalization of the IC (See Conjecture 3.1) for the commuting differential operators related with classical orthogonal polynomials.

We will also show that, under certain conditions, the new generalization is actually equivalent to a conjecture (See Conjecture 3.2) on integrals of polynomials over open subsets of B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with any (positive) measures. The latter conjecture turns out to be a natural variation of the Mathieu conjecture [Ma] (See Conjecture 1.2) from GG-finite functions on reductive Lie groups GG to polynomial functions over the open subsets B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} above. It also can be viewed as a natural variation of Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem [DK] (See Theorem 1.3) on Laurent polynomials with no constant terms.

To be more precise, let us first introduce the following notion which will provide a common ground for all the results and conjectures to be discussed in this paper.

Definition 1.1.

Let RR be any commutative ring and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} a commutative RR-algebra. We say that a RR-subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} if the following property holds: for any a,b∈𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}} with am∈ℳa^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have am​b∈ℳa^{m}b\in{\mathcal{M}} when m>>0m>>0, i.e. there exists N≥1N\geq 1 ((depending on aa and bb)) such that am​b∈ℳa^{m}b\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥Nm\geq N.

Note that, any ideal of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is automatically a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. But conversely, not all Mathieu subspaces are ideals. Actually, many Mathieu subspaces are not even closed under the product of the ambient algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. So the new notion can be viewed as a generalization of the notion of ideals. For more examples and general results on Mathieu subspaces, see Section 4.

The notion is named after Olivier Mathieu due to his following conjecture proposed in [Ma], 19951995.

Conjecture 1.2.

((The Mathieu Conjecture)) Let GG be a compact connected real Lie group with the Haar measure σ\sigma. Let ff a complex-valued GG-finite function over GG such that ∫Gfm​𝑑σ=0\int_{G}f^{m}\,d\sigma=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. Then, for any GG-finite function gg over GG, ∫Gfm​g​𝑑σ=0\int_{G}f^{m}g\,d\sigma=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Note that, in terms of the newly introduced notion of Mathieu subspaces, the Mathieu conjecture just claims that the ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-subspace of complex-valued GG-finite functions ff with ∫Gf​𝑑σ=0\int_{G}fd\sigma=0 is a Mathieu subspace of the ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} of complex-valued GG-finite functions over GG.

One of the motivations of the Mathieu conjecture is its connection with the Jacobian conjecture (See [BCW] and [E]). Actually, Mathieu also showed in [Ma] that his conjecture implies the Jacobian conjecture.

For later purposes, here we also point out that J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [DK] in 19981998 had proved the Mathieu conjecture for the case of tori, which now can be re-stated as follows.

Theorem 1.3.

((Duistermaat and van der Kallen)) Let z=(z1,z2𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸,z=(z_{1},z_{2}, ...,zn)...,z_{n}) be nn commutative free variables and ℳ{\mathcal{M}} the subspace of the Laurent polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z] consisting of the Laurent polynomials with no constant terms. Then ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z].

Another main motivation behind the new notion of Mathieu subspaces is the following so-called image conjecture (IC) proposed recently by the author in [Z3] on the images of commuting differential operators of polynomial algebras of order one with constant leading coefficients.

Let z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},...,z_{n}) be nn commutative free variables and ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] the algebra of polynomials in zz over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, set ∂i:=∂/∂zi\partial_{i}\!:=\partial/\partial z_{i}. We say a differential operator Φ\Phi of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] is of order one with constant leading coefficients if Φ=h(z)+∑i=1nci∂i\Phi=h(z)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\partial_{i} for some h⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]h(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and ci∈ℂc_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}. We denote by 𝔻⁡[z]{\mathbb{D}}[z] the subspace of all differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients. For any subset 𝒞={Φi|i∈I}{\mathcal{C}}=\{\Phi_{i}\,|\,i\in I\} of differential operators of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z], we set Im ​𝒞:=∑i∈I(Φi​ℂ​[z])\mbox{Im\,}{\mathcal{C}}\!:=\sum_{i\in I}(\Phi_{i}{\mathbb{C}}[z]) and call it the image of 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}. We say 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} is commuting if, for any i,j∈Ii,j\in I, Φi\Phi_{i} and Φj\Phi_{j} commute with each other.

With the notation fixed above, the IC can be re-stated as follows.

Conjecture 1.4.

((The Image Conjecture)) For any commuting subset 𝒞⊂𝔻⁡[z]{\mathcal{C}}\subset{\mathbb{D}}[z], Im ​𝒞\mbox{Im\,}{\mathcal{C}} is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Note that the IC, the Mathieu conjecture and also Conjectures 3.1–3.2 mentioned at the beginning of this subsection are all problems on whether or not certain subspaces are Mathieu subspaces. It is also the case for the Jacobian conjecture and, more generally, the vanishing conjecture [Z1], [Z2] on differential operators (of any order) with constant coefficients via their connections with the IC (See [Z3]). Furthermore, we can also include the well-known Dixmier conjecture [D] in the list since it has been shown, first by Y. Tsuchimoto [T] in 20052005 and later by A. Belov and M. Kontsevich [BK] and P. K. Adjamagbo and A. van den Essen [AE] in 20072007, that the Dixmier conjecture is actually equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture. The implication of the Jacobian conjecture from the Dixmier conjecture was actually proved much earlier by V. Kac (unpublished but see [BCW]) in 19821982.

Therefore, it is interesting and important to study Mathieu subspaces separately in a general and abstract setting. So we will also discuss more examples of Mathieu subspaces from other sources and derive some general results on this newly introduced notion (See Section 4).

1.2. Arrangement

In Subsection 2.1, we first recall some classical orthogonal polynomials and their related commuting differential operators (See Examples 2.2 and 2.4). We also fix some notations and summarize some facts that will be needed for the rest of this paper.

In Subsection 2.2, we consider the straightforward generalization of the IC for the commuting differential operators related with some multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials but without the constraints on the parameters required by the Jacobi polynomials. We will show in Proposition 2.6 that the straightforward generalization of the IC does not hold for these differential operators. But, if we generalize the IC in a different way, we will have a positive answer for these differential operators under the constraints on the parameters required by the Jacobi polynomials (See Corollary 2.10).

Another purpose of this subsection is to explain in a concrete setting the main ideas behind the generalization of the IC that will be formulated and discussed in Section 3. Some of the results of this subsection will also be needed later in Subsection 3.2.

In Subsection 3.1, we first formulate a generalization (See Conjecture 3.1) of the IC for the differential operators related with orthogonal polynomials, and also a conjecture (See Conjecture 3.2) on integrals of polynomials over open subsets B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with any positive measures. We show in Proposition 3.3 that the non-trivial case of Conjecture 3.1 is actually equivalent to some special cases of Conjecture 3.2. We also point out that Conjecture 3.2 in some sense can be viewed as a natural variation of the Mathieu conjecture (See Conjecture 1.2) and Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem (See Theorem 1.3).

In Subsection 3.2, we prove some cases of Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2. We also discuss a connection of Conjecture 3.2 with the polynomial moment problem which was first proposed by M. Briskin, J.-P. Francoise and Y. Yomdin in the series paper [BFY1]-[BFY5] and recently was solved by F. Pakovich and M. Muzychuk [PM].

In Section 4, we discuss Mathieu subspaces in the most general setting. Some examples of Mathieu subspaces from other sources will be given and some general results on this newly introduced notion will also be derived.

2. Differential Operators Related with Classical Orthogonal Polynomials

In this section, we first recall in Subsection 2.1 some classical orthogonal polynomials in one or more variables and their related differential operators. We also summarize in Lemma 2.5 some facts that will be needed in later sections.

The classical reference for one-variable orthogonal polynomials is [Sz] (see also [AS], [C], [Si]). For multi-variable orthogonal polynomials, see [DX], [Ko] and references therein. But here we will essentially follow the presentations given in [Z2] in terms of differential operators of certain localizations of polynomial algebras, and emphasize that the related differential operators are all commuting differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients. The presentation in [Z2] for multi-variable orthogonal polynomials will also be simplified here.

In Subsection 2.2, we consider the straightforward generalization of the image conjecture (IC) for some commuting differential operators of the Laurent polynomials. Up to changes of variables, these differential operators are related with some multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials (See Example 2.4). We show in Proposition 2.6 that the IC does not hold for these differential operators. But it does hold for the same differential operators if we generalize the IC in a different way (See Corollary 2.10).

2.1. Differential Operators Related with Classical Orthogonal Polynomials

First, let us recall the definition of classical orthogonal polynomials. In order to be consistent with the traditional notations of orthogonal polynomials, in this subsection we will use x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}) instead of z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{n}) to denote free commutative variables.

Definition 2.1.

Let BB be a non-empty open subset of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and w⁡(x)w(x) a real valued function defined over BB such that w⁡(x)≥0w(x)\geq 0 for any x∈Bx\in B and 0<∫Bw⁡(x)​𝑑x<∞0<\int_{B}w(x)dx<\infty. Assume further that ∫Bf⁡(x)​w​(x)​𝑑x\int_{B}f(x)w(x)dx is finite for any f⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x]f(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x]. A sequence of polynomials {uα​(x)|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}(x)\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} is said to be orthogonal over BB if

  1. (a)(a)

    deg⁡uα=|α|:=∑i=1nki\deg u_{\alpha}=|\alpha|:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{i} for any α=(k1,k2,…,kn)∈ℕn\alpha=(k_{1},k_{2},...,k_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

  2. (b)(b)

    the sequence {uα​(x)|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}(x)\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} forms an orthogonal basis of ℂ⁡[x]{\mathbb{C}}[x] with respect to the Hermitian form defined by

    (2.1) (f,g):=∫Bf​g¯​w​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle(f,g)\!:=\int_{B}f\bar{g}w(x)\,dx

    for any f,g∈ℂ⁡[x]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x], where g¯\bar{g} denotes the complex conjugate of the polynomial g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x].

The function w⁡(x)w(x) is called the weight function. For all classical orthogonal polynomials, w⁡(x)w(x) is smooth over BB but might have some singular points over the boundary of BB (See Examples 2.2 and 2.4 below). When the open set B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and w⁡(x)w(x) are clear in the context, we simply call the polynomials uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) in the definition above orthogonal polynomials. If the orthogonal polynomials uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) also satisfy ∫B|uα|2​w​(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{B}|u_{\alpha}|^{2}w(x)dx=1 for any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we call uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) orthonormal polynomials.

Note that, if uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are orthogonal polynomials, say, as in Definition 2.1, then, for any cα∈ℂ×c_{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times} (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}), cα​uαc_{\alpha}u_{\alpha} (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) are also orthogonal polynomials over BB with the same weight function w⁡(x)w(x).

An obvious way to construct orthogonal polynomials is to apply the Gram-Schmidt process. But, surprisingly, most of classical orthogonal polynomials can also be obtained by the following so-called Rodrigues’ formulas which, in terms of the notation as in Definition 2.1, can be stated as follows.

(2.2) uα​(x)=cα​w​(x)−1​∂|α|d​xα​(w⁡(x)​gα​(x)).\displaystyle u_{\alpha}(x)=c_{\alpha}w(x)^{-1}\frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}}{dx^{\alpha}}(w(x)g^{\alpha}(x)).

Note that, not all orthogonal polynomials defined in Definition 2.1 can be obtained by Rodrigues’ formulas. For example, the weight function w⁡(x)w(x) of some orthogonal polynomials may not even be differentiable.

Now, for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, let

Remark 2.3.

(a)(a) A very important special family of Jacobi polynomials are the Gegenbauer polynomials which are obtained by setting α=β=λ−1/2\alpha=\beta=\lambda-1/2 for some λ>−1/2\lambda>-1/2. The Gegenbauer polynomials are also called the ultraspherical polynomials in the literature.

(b)(b) For the special cases with λ=0,1,1/2\lambda=0,1,1/2, the Gegenbauer Polynomials are called the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, the second kind and the Legendre polynomials, respectively.

(c)(c) When n=2n=2, up to some non-zero constants the orthogonal polynomials Uα​(x)U_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕ2)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{2}) in Eq. (2.10)(\ref{n-Appell}) are also called Appell polynomials.

Note that, one important way to construct multi-variable orthogonal polynomials is to take cartesian products of orthogonal polynomials in one variable.

More precisely, let x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}) and {ui,m​(xi)|m≥0}\{u_{i,m}(x_{i})\,|\,m\geq 0\} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) be orthogonal polynomials over a subset Bi⊂ℝB_{i}\subset{\mathbb{R}} with weight function wi​(xi)w_{i}(x_{i}) over BiB_{i}. Let

(2.11) B\displaystyle B =B1×B2×⋯×Bn,\displaystyle=B_{1}\times B_{2}\times\cdots\times B_{n},
(2.12) w⁡(x)\displaystyle w(x) =w1(x1)w2(x2)⋯wn(xn),\displaystyle=w_{1}(x_{1})w_{2}(x_{2})\cdots w_{n}(x_{n}),
(2.13) uα​(x)\displaystyle u_{\alpha}(x) =u1,k1(x1)u2,k2(x2)⋯un,kn(xn)\displaystyle=u_{1,k_{1}}(x_{1})u_{2,k_{2}}(x_{2})\cdots u_{n,k_{n}}(x_{n})

for any α=(k1,k2,…,kn)∈ℕn\alpha=(k_{1},k_{2},...,k_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Then it is easy to see that {uα​(x)|α∈ℕ}\{u_{\alpha}(x)\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}\} are orthogonal polynomials over B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with respect to the weight function w⁡(x)w(x).

Furthermore, if, for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and m≥0m\geq 0, the orthogonal polynomial ui,m​(xi)=ci,m​Λim​(gim​(xi))u_{i,m}(x_{i})=c_{i,m}\Lambda_{i}^{m}(g_{i}^{m}(x_{i})) for some nonzero ci,m∈ℝc_{i,m}\in{\mathbb{R}}, gi​(x)∈ℂ⁡[xi]g_{i}(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{i}] and a differential operator Λi\Lambda_{i} of a localization of ℂ⁡[xi]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{i}]. Set Λ=(Λ1,Λ2,…,Λn)\Lambda=(\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},...,\Lambda_{n}) and g⁡(x)=(g1​(x1),g2​(x2),…,gn​(xn))g(x)=(g_{1}(x_{1}),g_{2}(x_{2}),...,g_{n}(x_{n})). Then, it is easy to see that Λ\Lambda is a commuting subset of differential operators of a localization of ℂ⁡[x]{\mathbb{C}}[x], and the orthogonal polynomials uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) over BB are given by

(2.14) uα​(x)=cα​Λα​(gα​(x)),\displaystyle u_{\alpha}(x)=c_{\alpha}\Lambda^{\alpha}(g^{\alpha}(x)),

where cα=∏i=1nci,αic_{\alpha}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,\alpha_{i}} for any α=(α1,α2,…,αn)∈ℕn\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...,\alpha_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

For later purposes, let us consider the multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials which, by Remark 2.3, also cover the multi-variable Gegenbauer, Chebyshev and Legendre orthogonal polynomials.

Example 2.4.

Let B=(−1,1)×n⊂ℝnB=(-1,1)^{\times n}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and α,β∈ℝn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with all the components αi,βi>−1\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}>-1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, set

(2.15) Λi:\displaystyle\Lambda_{i}\!: =dd​xi−αi​(1−xi)−1+βi​(1+xi)−1,\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dx_{i}}-\alpha_{i}(1-x_{i})^{-1}+\beta_{i}(1+x_{i})^{-1},

(2.18) Λα,β:\displaystyle\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\!: =(Λ1,Λ2,…,Λn),\displaystyle=(\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},...,\Lambda_{n}),
(2.19) g⁡(x):\displaystyle g(x)\!: =(g1​(x),g2​(x),…,gn​(x)).\displaystyle=(g_{1}(x),g_{2}(x),...,g_{n}(x)).

For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and m≥0m\geq 0, let Pmαi,βi​(x)P^{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}_{m}(x) be the mt​hm^{th} one-variable Jacobi polynomial in xix_{i} ((See Example 2.2, (3)(3))) with α=αi\alpha=\alpha_{i} and β=βi\beta=\beta_{i}. For any 𝐦=(m1,m2,…,mn)∈ℕn{\bf m}=(m_{1},m_{2},...,m_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, set

(2.20) P𝐦α,β​(x):=∏i=1nPmiαi,βi​(xi).\displaystyle P^{\alpha,\beta}_{\bf m}(x)\!:=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P^{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}_{m_{i}}(x_{i}).

Then, for any fixed α,β∈(ℝ>−1)×n\alpha,\beta\in({\mathbb{R}}^{>-1})^{\times n}, the sequence {P𝐦α,β​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{P^{\alpha,\beta}_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} forms a sequence of orthogonal polynomials over BB with the weight function given by Eq. (2.17)(\ref{MJP-W}). From Eq. (2.8)(\ref{JP-LP}), it is easy to see that the relation of {P𝐦α,β​(x)|𝐦∈ℕn}\{P^{\alpha,\beta}_{\bf m}(x)\,|\,{\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} with the commuting differential operators Λ\Lambda in Eq. (2.18)(\ref{MJP-Lambda}) and the polynomial g⁡(x)g(x) in Eq. (2.19)(\ref{MJP-g}) is given by

Finally, let us summarize the relations of orthogonal polynomials with commuting differential operators of order one with constant leading coefficients in the following lemma.

Lemma 2.5.

(a)(a) Up to some nonzero multiplicative scalars, all classical orthogonal polynomials {uα​(x)|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}(x)\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} above including those obtained by Cartesian products of classical orthogonal polynomials have the form in Eq. (2.4)(\ref{LaGa}) for some g⁡(x)=(g1​(x1),g2​(x2),…,gn​(xn))∈ℂ​[x]ng(x)=(g_{1}(x_{1}),g_{2}(x_{2}),...,g_{n}(x_{n}))\in{\mathbb{C}}[x]^{n} and differential operators Λ=(Λ1,Λ2,…,Λn)\Lambda=(\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},...,\Lambda_{n}) of some localizations ℬ{\mathcal{B}} of ℂ⁡[x]{\mathbb{C}}[x].

(b)(b) The set Λ\Lambda is a commuting subset of differential operators of ℬ{\mathcal{B}} of order one with constant leading coefficients.

(c)(c) For any nonzero α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, the orthogonal polynomials uα​(x)∈Im ′​Λ:=ℂ⁡[x]∩∑i=1n(Λi​ℂ​[x])u_{\alpha}(x)\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda\!:={\mathbb{C}}[x]\cap\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Lambda_{i}{\mathbb{C}}[x]).

Note that (a)(a) and (b)(b) follow immediately from the discussion in this subsection. (c)(c) follows from the fact that Λα​(gi​(x)​gα)\Lambda^{\alpha}(g_{i}(x)g^{\alpha}) for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, which can also be easily checked directly.

2.2. The Image Conjecture for the Differential Operators Related with the Multi-Variable Jacobi Orthogonal Polynomials

Considering the important roles of orthogonal polynomials played in so many different areas, it will be interesting to see if the image conjecture (IC), Conjecture 1.4, also holds for the commuting differential operators related with orthogonal polynomials.

In this subsection, we consider the straightforward generalization of the IC for the following family of commuting differential operators of Laurent polynomial algebras in a slightly more general setting, namely, with the base field ℂ{\mathbb{C}} replaced by integral domains over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. As we will see that the straightforward generalization of the IC is false for these differential operators (See Propositions 2.6 and 2.9). But another generalization of the IC for these differential operators under the constraints from the multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials actually holds (See Corollary 2.10).

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be any integral domain over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} and 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] the algebra of Laurent polynomials with coefficients in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. For any λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λn)∈ℂn\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{n})\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, we set Φλi:=∂i+λizi−1\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}\!:=\partial_{i}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{-1} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) and Φλ:=(Φλ1,Φλ2,…,Φλn)\Phi_{\lambda}\!:=(\Phi_{\lambda_{1}},\Phi_{\lambda_{2}},...,\Phi_{\lambda_{n}}). We will also view Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} as a commuting subset (instead of just an nn-tuple) of differential operators of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] of order one with constant leading coefficients.

Note that, the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} are essentially the differential operators related with the multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials P𝐦α,β​(x)P_{\bf m}^{\alpha,\beta}(x) (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) in Eq. (2.20) with α=0\alpha=0 or β=0\beta=0. For example, by setting α=0\alpha=0 and β=λ\beta=\lambda, and changing the variables xi→zi−1x_{i}\to z_{i}-1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), from Eqs. (2.15) and (2.18) we see that the differential operators Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta} related with the Jacobi polynomials will coincide with the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda}. Similarly, this is also the case when β=0\beta=0 if we set α=λ\alpha=\lambda and apply the changing of variables xi→zi+1x_{i}\to z_{i}+1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

But we emphasize that, unlike for the parameters α\alpha and β\beta of the Jacobi polynomials, here we do not require λi>−1\lambda_{i}>-1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) nor even λ∈ℝn\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} unless stated otherwise.

Now we fix any λ∈ℂn\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} and the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} as above, and set Im ​Φλ:=∑i=1n(Φλi​𝒜​[z−1,z])\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]). We also fix the following notation that will be used throughout the rest of this paper.

For any γ∈ℤn\gamma\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} and g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z], we denote by [zγ]​g​(z)[z^{\gamma}]g(z) the coefficient of the monomial zγz^{\gamma} in g⁡(z)g(z). For convenience, we also allow γ\gamma in the notation above to be any element of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, i.e. we set [zγ]​g​(z)=0[z^{\gamma}]g(z)=0 for any g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] and γ∈ℂn\ℤn\gamma\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\backslash{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}. In the case that [zγ]​g​(z)=0[z^{\gamma}]g(z)=0, we also say that g⁡(z)g(z) has no zγz^{\gamma} term.

With all the notations fixed above, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 2.6.

For any λ∈ℂn\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, denote by the abusing notation −λ−1-\lambda-1 the nn-tuple −λ−(1,1,…,1)-\lambda-(1,1,...,1). Then, we have

(a)(a) Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is the 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}-subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] consisting of the Laurent polynomials g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] with [z−λ−1]​g​(z)=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z)=0. In particular, Im ​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] if λ∉ℤn\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}.

(b)(b) Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] iff λ∉ℤn\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} or λ=(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda=(-1,-1,...,-1).

Proof:  We first prove the proposition for the case n=1n=1, i.e. for the one-variable case.

For any g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z], consider the ordinary differential equation with the unknown function f⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]:

(2.22) Φλ​f=f′+λ​z−1​f=g.\displaystyle\Phi_{\lambda}f=f^{\prime}+\lambda z^{-1}f=g.

The equation above can be solved by the following standard trick in ODE. First, we view the equation as a differential equation for elements of 𝒜⁡[z±λ,z±1]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{\pm\lambda},z^{\pm 1}], and set f~​(z):=zλ​f​(z)∈𝒜⁡[z±λ,z±1]\tilde{f}(z)\!:=z^{\lambda}f(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{\pm\lambda},z^{\pm 1}]. Then f⁡(z)=z−λ​f~​(z)f(z)=z^{-\lambda}\tilde{f}(z). Plug this expression of f⁡(z)f(z) in Eq. (2.22), it is easy to check that f~​(z)\tilde{f}(z) satisfies the following equation:

z−λ​f~′=g.\displaystyle z^{-\lambda}\tilde{f}^{\prime}=g.

Therefore, we have f~​(z)=∫zλ​g​(z)​𝑑z\tilde{f}(z)=\int z^{\lambda}g(z)\,dz and

(2.23) f⁡(z)\displaystyle f(z) =z−λ​∫zλ​g​(z)​𝑑z.\displaystyle=z^{-\lambda}\int z^{\lambda}g(z)\,dz.

From the arguments, we see that any solution f∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]f\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] of Eq. (2.22) must be given by Eq. (2.23) up to an z−λz^{-\lambda} term. But, conversely, the RHS of Eq. (2.23) does not necessarily produce an element of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] unless zλ​g​(z)z^{\lambda}g(z) has no z−1z^{-1} term, i.e. the residue Res​zλ​g​(z)=0\mbox{\rm Res}\,z^{\lambda}g(z)=0.

Therefore, the differential equation Eq. (2.22) has a Laurent polynomial solution f⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]f(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] iff Res​zλ​g​(z)=0\mbox{\rm Res}\,z^{\lambda}g(z)=0 iff [z−λ−1]​g​(z)=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z)=0. Hence, we have (a)(a) of the proposition for the case n=1n=1.

To show (b)(b) for the case n=1n=1, let us look at all the values of λ∈ℂ\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}} such that Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

First, if λ∉ℤ\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}, by (a)(a) Im ​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] which is obviously a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

Consider the case λ∈ℤ\lambda\in{\mathbb{Z}}. If −λ−1≠0-\lambda-1\neq 0, i.e. λ≠−1\lambda\neq-1. Then, by statement (a)(a) for the case n=1n=1, we have, 1∈Im ​Φλ1\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} and Im ​Φλ≠𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}\neq{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]. By the general property of Mathieu subspaces given in Lemma 4.5 in Section 4, Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is not a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

A more convincing counter-example for this case can be constructed as follows. Set

(2.24) v⁡(z):\displaystyle v(z)\!: =z−λ−1\displaystyle=z^{-\lambda-1}
(2.25) u⁡(z):\displaystyle u(z)\!: ={1+z−λ if ​λ<−1;1+z−λ−2 if ​λ>−1.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1+z^{-\lambda}&\mbox{ if }\lambda<-1;\\ 1+z^{-\lambda-2}&\mbox{ if }\lambda>-1.\end{cases}

Then, it is easy to check that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have [z−λ−1]​um=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]u^{m}=0 and [z−λ−1]​(um​v)=z−λ−1[z^{-\lambda-1}](u^{m}v)=z^{-\lambda-1}. By statement (a)(a) for the case n=1n=1, we have that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, um∈Im ​Φλu^{m}\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} but um​v∉Im ​Φλu^{m}v\not\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}.

Next, consider the case λ=−1\lambda=-1. By (a)(a), we know that Im ​Φλ=−1\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda=-1} is the 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}-subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] consisting of Laurent polynomials with no constant terms. In the case that 𝒜=ℂ{\mathcal{A}}={\mathbb{C}}, (b)(b) follows directly from Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3.

In the case that 𝒜≠ℂ{\mathcal{A}}\neq{\mathbb{C}}, (b)(b) also follows from Theorem 1.3 via Lefschetz’s principle since, whenever we fix a⁡(z),b⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]a(z),b(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] with am​(z)a^{m}(z) has no constant term for any m≥1m\geq 1, to show that am​ba^{m}b has no constant term when m>>0m>>0, we may replace 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} by the field KK generated by the (finitely many) coefficients of a⁡(z)a(z) and b⁡(z)b(z) over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, which can be embedded in ℂ{\mathbb{C}} as a subfield.

Therefore, we have proved the proposition for the case n=1n=1. Now we assume n≥2n\geq 2.

For convenience, throughout the rest of the proof, we denote by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} the subalgebra of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] of Laurent polynomials in ziz_{i} (2≤i≤n)(2\leq i\leq n) with coefficients in 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Note that 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] may be viewed as the Laurent polynomial algebra in z1z_{1} over 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}, i.e. we have 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]=𝒰⁡[z1−1,z1]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]={\mathcal{U}}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}].

First, assume that λ∉ℤn\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}. Then there exists 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that λi∉ℤ\lambda_{i}\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}. Without losing any generality, we assume λ1∉ℤ\lambda_{1}\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}. By statement (a)(a) for the one-variable case with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and λ\lambda by λ1\lambda_{1}, we have

Φλ1​(𝒰⁡[z1−1,z1])=𝒰⁡[z1−1,z1]=𝒜⁡[z−1,z].\displaystyle\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{U}}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}])={\mathcal{U}}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}]={\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

Since Φλ1​(𝒰⁡[z1−1,z1])=Φλ1​(𝒜⁡[z−1,z])⊂Im ​Φλ\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{U}}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}])=\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z])\subset\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}, from the equation above, we have Im ​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

Now assume λ∈ℤn\lambda\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}. We first show that zβ∈Im ​Φλz^{\beta}\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} for any β∈ℤn\beta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} with β≠−λ−1\beta\neq-\lambda-1.

Pick up any β≠−λ−1∈ℤn\beta\neq-\lambda-1\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, there exists 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that the it​hi^{th} component βi\beta_{i} of β\beta is different from −λi−1-\lambda_{i}-1. We assume β1≠−λ1−1\beta_{1}\neq-\lambda_{1}-1 (the proof for other cases is similar). Then, by statement (a)(a) for the one-variable case with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and λ\lambda by λ1\lambda_{1}, we have

zβ=(z2β2z3β3⋯znβn)z1β1∈Φλ1(𝒰[z1−1,z1])=Φλ1(𝒜[z−1,z])⊂Im Φλ.\displaystyle z^{\beta}=(z_{2}^{\beta_{2}}z_{3}^{\beta_{3}}\cdots z_{n}^{\beta_{n}})z_{1}^{\beta_{1}}\in\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{U}}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}])=\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z])\subset\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}.

Consequently, we see that any g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] with [z−λ−1]​g​(z)=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z)=0 lies in Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}. Conversely, for any g⁡(z)∈Im ​Φλg(z)\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}, we write g⁡(z)g(z) as

(2.26) g⁡(z)=∑i=1nΦλi​fi​(z)\displaystyle g(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}f_{i}(z)

for some fi​(z)∈𝒜⁡[z−1,z]f_{i}(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

By statement (a)(a) for the one-variable case with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} and λ\lambda by λ1\lambda_{1}, we see that Φλ1​f1​(z)\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}f_{1}(z) in Eq. (2.26) has no zγz^{\gamma} term for any γ∈ℤn\gamma\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} with the first component γ1=−λ1−1\gamma_{1}=-\lambda_{1}-1. Hence, for the similar reason, for any 2≤i≤n2\leq i\leq n, Φλi​fi​(z)\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}f_{i}(z) in Eq. (2.26) can not have the zγz^{\gamma} term for any γ∈ℤn\gamma\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} with the it​hi^{th} component γi=−λi−1\gamma_{i}=-\lambda_{i}-1. Therefore, by Eq. (2.26) we see that g⁡(z)g(z) can not have any z−λ−1z^{-\lambda-1} term.

Combining the results in the last two paragraphs, we have statement (a)(a) of the proposition.

Next we show statement (b)(b). First, if λ∉ℤn\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, by (a)(a) we have Im ​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] which is obviously a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

Assume that λ∈ℤn\lambda\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} but λ≠(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda\neq(-1,-1,...,-1). Since −λ−1≠0∈ℕn-\lambda-1\neq 0\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, by statement (a)(a), we have, 1∈Im ​Φλ1\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} and Im ​Φλ≠𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}\neq{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]. By Lemma 4.5 in Section 4, Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is not a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z].

Finally, consider the case λ=(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda=(-1,-1,...,-1). Similarly as for the one variable case, by Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3, and Lefschetz’s principle, it is easy to see that Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z] in this case.  □\Box

Remark 2.7.

From Proposition 2.6, we see that ((the straightforward generalization of)) the IC for the Laurent polynomial algebras does not always hold.

But, on the other hand, it is still interesting to see, for which commuting differential operators of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z] or any localization of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z], the IC does hold. For example, for the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} with λ=(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda=(-1,-1,...,-1), the IC is actually equivalent to Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3. Even more mysteriously, among all the cases that Im ​Φλ≠𝒜⁡[z−1,z]\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}\neq{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z], this is the only case that the IC holds.

Next let us consider the IC for the polynomial algebra 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] (instead of 𝒜⁡[z−1,z]{\mathcal{A}}[z^{-1},z]) and the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} (even though 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] is not closed under the action of Φλ\Phi_{\lambda}). But, first, we need prove the following lemma.

Lemma 2.8.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} (λ∈ℂn)(\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}) and Im ​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} as in Proposition 2.6. Then, for any g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z], g⁡(z)∈Im ​Φλg(z)\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda} iff g⁡(z)∈∑i=1n(Φλi​𝒜​[z])g(z)\in\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z]).

Proof:  Note that the (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of the lemma is trivial. We use induction on n≥1n\geq 1 to show the other part.

First, assume n=1n=1 and g⁡(z)∈Im ​Φλg(z)\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}. Then, by Proposition 2.6, (a)(a), we have [z−λ−1]​g​(z)=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z)=0. By writing g⁡(z)g(z) as a linear combination of monomials zkz^{k} (k∈ℕ)(k\in{\mathbb{N}}) over 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, it is easy to check that Eq. (2.23)(\ref{P4.2.1-pe5}) has a polynomial solution f⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z]. Since Φλ​f​(z)=g⁡(z)\Phi_{\lambda}f(z)=g(z) as shown in the proof of Proposition 2.6, the lemma holds in this case.

Next assume the lemma holds for the n−1n-1 case and consider the nn-variable case.

Note first that, for any λ∈ℂn\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} and g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z], there exist u⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z2,z3,…,zn]u(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z_{2},z_{3},...,z_{n}] and v⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]v(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z] such that [zγ]​v​(z)=0[z^{\gamma}]v(z)=0 for any γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with the first component γ1=−λ1−1\gamma_{1}=-\lambda_{1}-1 and

(2.27) g⁡(z)=z1−λ1−1​u​(z)+v⁡(z).\displaystyle g(z)=z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z)+v(z).

Now further assume g⁡(z)∈Im ​Φλg(z)\in\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}. Then, by Proposition 2.6, (a)(a), we have [z−λ−1]​g​(z)=0[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z)=0. We show below that both terms on the right hand side of Eq. (2.27) lie in ∑i=1n(Φλi​𝒜​[z])\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z]).

First, if −λ1−1∉ℕ-\lambda_{1}-1\not\in{\mathbb{N}}, we have u⁡(z)=0u(z)=0. Otherwise, set 𝒜′:=𝒜⁡[z1]{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\!:={\mathcal{A}}[z_{1}] and z′′:=(z2,…,zn)z^{\prime\prime}\!:=(z_{2},...,z_{n}). We view u⁡(z)u(z) and also z1−λ1−1​u​(z)z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z) as polynomials in z′′z^{\prime\prime} over the integral domain 𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}. Note that, the coefficient of the monomial z2−λ2−1⋯zn−λn−1z_{2}^{-\lambda_{2}-1}\cdots z_{n}^{-\lambda_{n}-1} in u⁡(z)∈𝒜′​[z′′]u(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}[z^{\prime\prime}] is same as [z−λ−1]​g​(z)[z^{-\lambda-1}]g(z) which is equal to zero. Hence the coefficient of z2−λ2−1⋯zn−λn−1z_{2}^{-\lambda_{2}-1}\cdots z_{n}^{-\lambda_{n}-1} in z1−λ1−1​u​(z)∈𝒜′​[z′′]z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}[z^{\prime\prime}] is also equal to zero.

Apply Proposition 2.6, (a)(a) to z1−λ1−1​u​(z)∈𝒜′​[z′′]z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}[z^{\prime\prime}] with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}, we know that z1−λ1−1​u​(z)∈∑i=2n(Φλi​𝒜′​[z2±,…,zn±])z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z)\in\sum_{i=2}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}[z_{2}^{\pm},...,z_{n}^{\pm}]). Then, by applying the induction assumption to z1−λ1−1​u​(z)z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z) with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒜′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}, we have, z1−λ1−1​u​(z)∈∑i=2n(Φλi​𝒜′​[z2,…,zn])=∑i=2n(Φλi​𝒜​[z])z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}u(z)\in\sum_{i=2}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}[z_{2},...,z_{n}])=\sum_{i=2}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z]).

Second, set 𝒜′′:=𝒜⁡[z2,…,zn]{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}\!:={\mathcal{A}}[z_{2},...,z_{n}]. Then, viewing v⁡(z)v(z) as a polynomial in z1z_{1} over the integral domain 𝒜′′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}, we have [z1−λ1−1]​v​(z)=0[z_{1}^{-\lambda_{1}-1}]v(z)=0. By Proposition 2.6, (a)(a) with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒜′′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}, v⁡(z)∈Φλ1​(𝒜′′​[z1−1,z1])v(z)\in\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}[z_{1}^{-1},z_{1}]). Applying the lemma for the case n=1n=1 to v⁡(z)v(z) with 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} replaced by 𝒜′′{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}, we have v⁡(z)∈Φλ1​(𝒜′′​[z1])=Φλ1​(𝒜⁡[z])v(z)\in\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}^{\prime\prime}[z_{1}])=\Phi_{\lambda_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}[z]). Then, by Eq. (2.27), we have g⁡(z)∈∑i=1n(Φλi​𝒜​[z])g(z)\in\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z]), and the lemma follows.  □\Box

Proposition 2.9.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} (λ∈ℂn)(\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}) as in Proposition 2.6. Set

(2.28) Im ′​Φλ:=𝒜⁡[z]∩∑i=1n(Φλi​𝒜​[z]).\displaystyle\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}\!:={\mathcal{A}}[z]\cap\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Phi_{\lambda_{i}}{\mathcal{A}}[z]).

Then, (a)(a) Im ′​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z] iff λ∉(ℤ<0)n\lambda\not\in({\mathbb{Z}}^{<0})^{n}, where ℤ<0{\mathbb{Z}}^{<0} denotes the set of all negative integers.

(b)(b) Im ′​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] iff λ∉(ℤ<0)n\lambda\not\in({\mathbb{Z}}^{<0})^{n} or λ=(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda=(-1,-1,...,-1).

Proof:  Note first that, by Eq. (2.28) and Lemma 2.8, it is easy to see that

(2.29) Im ′​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z]∩Im ​Φλ.\displaystyle\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z]\cap\mbox{Im\,}\Phi_{\lambda}.

If λ∉ℤn\lambda\not\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, by Proposition 2.6, (a)(a) and the equation above, we have that Im ′​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z].

Assume λ∈ℤn\lambda\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} and set α:=−λ−(1,1,…,1)\alpha\!:=-\lambda-(1,1,...,1). By Proposition 2.6, (a)(a) and Eq. (2.29), we know that Im ′​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda} is the 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}-subspace of polynomials with no zαz^{\alpha} term.

If λ∉(ℤ<0)n\lambda\not\in({\mathbb{Z}}^{<0})^{n}, i.e. λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 for some 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, then we have α∉ℕn\alpha\not\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} and hence Im ′​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z].

Now assume λ∈(ℤ<0)n\lambda\in({\mathbb{Z}}^{<0})^{n} but λ≠(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda\neq(-1,-1,...,-1). Then there exists 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n such that λj≤−2\lambda_{j}\leq-2. Note that, in this case α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} but α≠0\alpha\neq 0. Consequently, we have, 1∈Im ′​Φλ1\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda} and Im ′​Φλ≠𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}\neq{\mathcal{A}}[z]. Then, by Lemma 4.5 in Section 4, Im ′​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda} is not a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

Finally, if λ=(−1,−1,…,−1)\lambda=(-1,-1,...,-1), then α=0\alpha=0 and Im ′​Φλ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda} is the ideal of all polynomials with no constant terms. So in this case Im ′​Φλ≠𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}\neq{\mathcal{A}}[z] but is the ideal of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z] generated by ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Hence it is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

So we have exhausted all possible choices of λ∈ℂn\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. Combining all the results above, it is easy to see that both (a)(a) and (b)(b) of the proposition hold.  □\Box

As pointed out at the beginning of this subsection, up to some changes of variables, the differential operators Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} are same as the differential operators Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta} in Eq. (2.18) related with the multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials P𝐦α,βP^{\alpha,\beta}_{\bf m} (𝐦∈ℕn)({\bf m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) in Eq. (2.20) with α=λ\alpha=\lambda and β=0\beta=0 or α=0\alpha=0 and β=λ\beta=\lambda.

Note that, the constraints on the parameters α\alpha and β\beta of the Jacobi polynomials are α,β∈ℝn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and the components αi,βi>−1\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}>-1 (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Now, if we put the same constraints on λ\lambda, then, by Proposition 2.9, it is easy to see that we have the following corollary.

Corollary 2.10.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and Φλ\Phi_{\lambda} as in Proposition 2.6. Assume further that λ∈ℝn\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and λi>−1\lambda_{i}>-1 for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Then, Im ′​Φλ=𝒜⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\lambda}={\mathcal{A}}[z] and hence is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

3. Generalizations of the Image Conjecture

Motivated by the discussions in Subsection 2.2, we first formulate in Subsection 3.1 a generalization (See Conjecture 3.1) of the IC for the commuting differential operators related with orthogonal polynomials. We also show that, beside a trivial case, Conjecture 3.1 is actually equivalent to a special case of another conjecture, Conjecture 3.2, on integrals of polynomials over open subsets of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with any positive measures. As we will see that Conjecture 3.2 can also be viewed as a natural variation of the Mathieu conjecture, Conjecture 1.2, and Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3.

In Subsection 3.2, we will prove some cases of Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2. We will also discuss a connection of Conjecture 3.2 with the so-called polynomial moment problem.

3.1. The Generalized Image Conjecture

First, we propose the following generalization of the IC for the commuting differential operators related with classical orthogonal polynomials.

Conjecture 3.1.

Let B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, w⁡(z)w(z) and {uα|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} as in Definition 2.1 with xx replaced by zz. Assume further that the orthogonal polynomials {uα|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} can be obtained via Eq. (2.4)(\ref{LaGa}) for some commuting differential operators Λ=(Λ1,Λ2,…,Λn)\Lambda=(\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},...,\Lambda_{n}) of a localization of the polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z]. Set

(3.1) Im ′​Λ:=ℂ⁡[z]​⋂∑i=1n(Λi​ℂ​[z]).\displaystyle\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda\!:={\mathbb{C}}[z]\,\bigcap\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\Lambda_{i}{\mathbb{C}}[z]).

Then, Im ′​Λ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Note first that, when Λ\Lambda are differential operators of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] (instead of a localization of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z]), we have, Im ′​Λ=Im ​Λ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda=\mbox{Im\,}\Lambda. Therefore, the conjecture above can be viewed as a generalization of the image conjecture, Conjecture 1.4, to the differential operators related with classical orthogonal polynomials.

Note also that, by Lemma 2.5, (c)(c), Im ′​Λ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda has co-dimension in ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] zero or one depending on whether u0​(z)u_{0}(z) lies in Im ′​Λ\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda or not. Since u0​(z)u_{0}(z) is a nonzero constant, we have Im ′​Λ=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda={\mathbb{C}}[z] iff 1∈Im′​Λ1\in\mbox{Im}^{\prime}\Lambda.

Therefore, if 1∈Im′​Λ1\in\mbox{Im}^{\prime}\Lambda, we have Im ′​Λ=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda={\mathbb{C}}[z], and hence Conjecture 3.1 holds trivially in this case. If 1∉Im ′​Λ1\not\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda, we have

(3.2) Im′​Λ=Spanℂ​{uα​(z)|α≠0}.\displaystyle\mbox{Im}^{\prime}\Lambda=\mbox{Span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{u_{\alpha}(z)\,|\,\alpha\neq 0\}.

In this case, Conjecture 3.1 turns out to be equivalent to a special case of the following conjecture.

Conjecture 3.2.

Let BB be any non-empty open subset of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and σ\sigma any positive measure such that ∫Bg⁡(z)​𝑑σ\int_{B}g(z)\,d\sigma is finite for any g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]. Let ℳB​(σ){\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma) be the subspace of all polynomials f⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] such that ∫Bf⁡(x)​𝑑σ=0\int_{B}f(x)\,d\sigma=0. Then ℳB​(σ){\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma) is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Proposition 3.3.

Let B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, w⁡(z)w(z) and Λ\Lambda be as in Conjecture 3.1. Let σ\sigma be the measure on BB such that d​σ=w⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=w(z)dz. Assume further that 1∉Im ′​Λ1\not\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda. Then, we have

(a)(a) Im ′​Λ=ℳB​(σ)\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda={\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma).

(b)(b) Conjecture 3.1 for the differential operators Λ\Lambda is equivalent to Conjecture 3.2 for the open subset B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with the measure σ\sigma.

Proof:  First it is easy to see that (b)(b) follows directly from (a)(a).

To show (a)(a), choose any f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and write it (uniquely) as f⁡(z)=∑α∈ℕncα​uα​(z)f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}c_{\alpha}u_{\alpha}(z) with cα∈ℂc_{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{C}}. Then, by Eq. (3.2) and the assumption that 1∉Im ′​Λ1\not\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda, we have that, f⁡(z)∈Im ′​Λf(z)\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda iff c0=0c_{0}=0.

On the other hand, since {uα|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} is an orthogonal basis of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] with respect to the Hermitian form defined in Definition 2.1, for any α≠0\alpha\neq 0, we have

(3.3) ∫Buα​(z)​w​(z)​𝑑z=u¯0−1​∫Buα​(z)​u¯0​w​(z)​𝑑z=0.\displaystyle\int_{B}u_{\alpha}(z)w(z)dz=\bar{u}_{0}^{-1}\int_{B}u_{\alpha}(z)\bar{u}_{0}\,w(z)dz=0.

Therefore, we have

∫Bf⁡(z)​𝑑σ=∫Bf⁡(z)​w​(z)​𝑑z=c0​∫u0​(z)​w​(z)​𝑑z=c0​u0​∫Bw⁡(z)​𝑑z.\displaystyle\int_{B}f(z)\,d\sigma=\int_{B}f(z)w(z)dz=c_{0}\int u_{0}(z)w(z)dz=c_{0}u_{0}\int_{B}w(z)\,dz.

Since u0u_{0} and ∫w⁡(z)​𝑑z\int w(z)\,dz are nonzero constants, we have that, f​(z)∈ℳB​(σ)f(z)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma) iff c0=0c_{0}=0.

Combining the results above, we have Im ′​Λ=ℳB​(σ)\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda={\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma) which is (a)(a) of the proposition.  □\Box

Remark 3.4.

For the special case that 1∈Im ′​Λ1\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda, as pointed out above Conjecture 3.1 holds trivially. But in this case, Conjecture 3.2, even for the measures d​σ=w⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=w(z)dz given by the weight functions w⁡(z)w(z) of classical orthogonal polynomials, can still be highly non-trivial. See Subsection 3.2 for more discussions.

Several more remarks on Conjecture 3.2 are as follows.

First, Conjecture 3.2 can be viewed as a variation of the Mathieu conjecture, Conjecture 1.2, with the reductive Lie group GG replaced by an open subset B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}; the Haar measure by any positive measure σ\sigma; and GG-finite functions by polynomials. Furthermore, by Eq. (3.2) and Proposition 3.3, (a)(a), we see that Conjecture 3.2 with d​σ=w⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=w(z)dz can also be viewed as a natural variation of Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3, with the basis of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] formed by monomials zαz^{\alpha} (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) replaced by the basis formed by the orthogonal polynomials uα​(z)u_{\alpha}(z) (α∈ℕn)(\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}). More precisely, Conjecture 3.2 with d​σ=w⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=w(z)dz can be re-stated as follows.

Conjecture 3.5.

Let {uα|α∈ℕn}\{u_{\alpha}\,|\,\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\} be a sequence of orthogonal polynomials over B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with the weight function w⁡(z)w(z). Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the subspace of f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] whose constant term ((the coefficient of u0u_{0})) in the unique expansion of f⁡(z)f(z) in terms of uα​(z)u_{\alpha}(z)’s is equal to zero. Then ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a Mathieu subspace of the polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Of course, a shorter way to state the conjecture above is that the subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} spanned by the orthogonal polynomials uα​(z)u_{\alpha}(z) (α≠0)(\alpha\neq 0) over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} is a Mathieu subspace of the polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

The second remark is that Conjecture 3.2 in general does not hold for analytic functions.

Example 3.6.

Let B=(0, 1)⊂ℝB=(0,\,1)\subset{\mathbb{R}} and d​σ=d​zd\sigma=dz. Let f⁡(x)=e2​π​−1​zf(x)=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\,z} and g⁡(z)=zg(z)=z. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

∫01fm​(x)​𝑑σ=∫01e2​m​π​−1​z​𝑑z=0.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}f^{m}(x)\,d\sigma=\int_{0}^{1}e^{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}\,z}\,dz=0.

But

∫01fm​(z)​g​(z)​𝑑σ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}f^{m}(z)g(z)\,d\sigma =∫01z​e2​m​π​−1​z​𝑑z\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}ze^{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}\,z}\,dz
=12​m​π​−1​(z​e2​m​π​−1​z|01−∫01e2​m​π​−1​z​𝑑z)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}}\left(\left.ze^{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}\,z}\right|_{0}^{1}-\int_{0}^{1}e^{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}\,z}\,dz\right)
=12​m​π​−1≠0.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2m\pi\sqrt{-1}}\neq 0.

The third remark is that Conjecture 3.2 does not hold without the positivity assumption on the measure σ\sigma.

Example 3.7.

Let B=(−1,1)⊂ℝB=(-1,1)\subset{\mathbb{R}} and d​σ=z​d​zd\sigma=zdz. Let f⁡(z)=z2f(z)=z^{2} and g⁡(z)=zg(z)=z. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

∫−11fm​(z)​𝑑σ=∫−11z2​m+1​𝑑z=0\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}f^{m}(z)\,d\sigma=\int_{-1}^{1}z^{2m+1}\,dz=0

But

∫−11fm​(z)​g​(z)​𝑑σ=∫−11z2​m+2​𝑑z=22​m+3≠0\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}f^{m}(z)g(z)\,d\sigma=\int_{-1}^{1}z^{2m+2}\,dz=\frac{2}{2m+3}\neq 0

Finally, one interesting observation about the example above is as follows. Even though Conjecture 3.2 fails for this example, if we consider the differential operator Λ\Lambda related with the “weight” function w⁡(z)=zw(z)=z as in Eq. (2.3), namely,

Λ=dd​z+w−1​(z)​d​w​(z)d​z=dd​z+z−1,\displaystyle\Lambda=\frac{d}{dz}+w^{-1}(z)\frac{dw(z)}{dz}=\frac{d}{dz}+z^{-1},

then, by Corollary 2.10, we see that Conjecture 3.1 (formally) for the differential operator Λ\Lambda above still holds.

3.2. Some Cases of Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2

Despite the simple appearances of Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2, there are only few cases that are known for these two conjectures.

First, for the differential operators related with the multi-variable Jacobi orthogonal polynomials ((See Example 2.4)), we have the following proposition.

Proposition 3.8.

Let Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta} be the commuting differential operators defined in Eq. (2.18)(\ref{MJP-Lambda}) ((with xx replaced by zz)) related with the Jacobi orthogonal polynomials. Assume further that there exists 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that αi=0\alpha_{i}=0 or βi=0\beta_{i}=0. Then Im ′​Λα,β=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}={\mathbb{C}}[z], and hence Conjecture 3.1 holds for Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}.

Proof:  Without losing any generality, we may assume that α1=0\alpha_{1}=0 or β1=0\beta_{1}=0. Here we only prove the case that β1=0\beta_{1}=0. The proof of the case that α1=0\alpha_{1}=0 is similar.

Under the assumption above, the first component Λ1\Lambda_{1} of Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta} in Eq. (2.18)(\ref{MJP-Lambda}) is the differential operator Λ1=∂1−α1(1−z1)−1\Lambda_{1}=\partial_{1}-\alpha_{1}(1-z_{1})^{-1}. Now we apply the change of variables z1→z1+1z_{1}\to z_{1}+1 and zi→ziz_{i}\to z_{i} for any 2≤i≤n2\leq i\leq n, then Λ1\Lambda_{1} becomes the differential operator Φα1=∂1+α1z1−1\Phi_{\alpha_{1}}=\partial_{1}+\alpha_{1}z_{1}^{-1}.

𝒜⁡[z1]∩Φα1​(𝒜⁡[z1])=𝒜⁡[z1].\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}[z_{1}]\cap\Phi_{\alpha_{1}}({\mathcal{A}}[z_{1}])={\mathcal{A}}[z_{1}].

Since 𝒜⁡[z1]=ℂ⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z_{1}]={\mathbb{C}}[z], we have

Im ′​Φα1=ℂ⁡[z]∩Φα1​(ℂ⁡[z])=ℂ⁡[z].\displaystyle\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Phi_{\alpha_{1}}={\mathbb{C}}[z]\cap\Phi_{\alpha_{1}}({\mathbb{C}}[z])={\mathbb{C}}[z].

Hence we also have Im ′​Λ1=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{1}={\mathbb{C}}[z]. Since Im ′​Λ1⊂Im ′​Λα,β\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{1}\subset\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}, we have Im ′​Λα,β=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}={\mathbb{C}}[z].  □\Box

Next let us consider the differential operators Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} (α∈(ℝ>−1)×nCLOSE(\alpha\in({\mathbb{R}}^{>-1})^{\times n}) related with the multi-variable Laguerre orthogonal polynomials. (3.4) Λα=(Λα1,Λα2,…,Λαn),\displaystyle\Lambda_{\alpha}=(\Lambda_{\alpha_{1}},\Lambda_{\alpha_{2}},...,\Lambda_{\alpha_{n}}),

where, for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

(3.5) Λαi=∂i+αizi−1−1.\displaystyle\Lambda_{\alpha_{i}}=\partial_{i}+\alpha_{i}z_{i}^{-1}-1.
Proposition 3.9.

Let Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} (α∈(ℝ>−1)×n)(\alpha\in({\mathbb{R}}^{>-1})^{\times n}) be the commuting differential operators defined above. Then, Im ′​Λα=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha}={\mathbb{C}}[z] iff αi=0\alpha_{i}=0 for some 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Hence, Conjectures 3.1 holds for Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} under this condition.

Proof:  (⇐)(\Leftarrow) Without losing any generality, we may assume that α1=0\alpha_{1}=0. Then, by Eq. (2.6), we have Λα1=0=∂1−1\Lambda_{\alpha_{1}=0}=\partial_{1}-1. Since Λα1=0​(−1)=1\Lambda_{\alpha_{1}=0}(-1)=1, we have 1∈Im ′​(Λα1=0)⊂Im ′​Λα1\in\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}(\Lambda_{\alpha_{1}=0})\subset\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha}. Then, by Lemma 2.5, (c)(c), we have Im ′​Λα=ℂ⁡[z]\mbox{Im\,}^{\prime}\Lambda_{\alpha}={\mathbb{C}}[z].

which is a contradiction since e−∑i=1nzi2e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}} is continuous and positive everywhere on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.  □\Box

Now let us consider some cases of Conjecture 3.2.

Proposition 3.11.

Conjecture 3.2 holds for any open B⊂ℝnB\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with any atomic measure σ\sigma which is supported at finitely many points of BB.

for any m≥1m\geq 1

Hence, for any m≥1m\geq 1, fm​gf^{m}g also satisfies Eq. (3.16) and lies in ℳB​(σ){\mathcal{M}}_{B}(\sigma). Therefore, Conjecture 3.2 holds for f⁡(z)f(z).

Assume f⁡(ui)f(u_{i}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) are not all zero. Let {c1,c2,…,cs}\{c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{s}\} be the set of all distinct nonzero values of f⁡(z)f(z) attained over SS. For any 1≤j≤s1\leq j\leq s, let SjS_{j} be the subset of elements of u∈Su\in S such that f⁡(u)=cjf(u)=c_{j} and kjk_{j} the cardinal number of SjS_{j}. Then, Eq. (3.17) can be re-written as

(3.18) 0=∑i=1kfm​(ui)​σ​(ui)=∑j=1scjm​∑u∈Sjσ⁡(u),\displaystyle 0=\sum_{i=1}^{k}f^{m}(u_{i})\sigma(u_{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_{j}^{m}\sum_{u\in S_{j}}\sigma(u),

for any 1≤j≤s1\leq j\leq s.

But this is a contradiction since σ⁡(ui)>0\sigma(u_{i})>0 for any 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k.  □\Box

Next, let us consider Conjecture 3.2 for the Jacobi orthogonal polynomials. Contrast to Conjecture 3.1 for the Jacobi polynomials (See Proposition 3.8), the only case of Conjecture 3.2 that we know is the case of the one-variable Jacobi polynomials with α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0. In this case the weight function w⁡(z)≡1w(z)\equiv 1. Note that, by Remark 2.3, (b)(b), the Jacobi polynomials in this case are actually the Legendre polynomials.

Proposition 3.12.

Let a,b∈ℝa,b\in{\mathbb{R}} with a>ba>b and d​σ=d​zd\sigma=dz. Then Conjecture 3.2 holds for open interval B:=(a,b)⊂ℝB\!:=(a,b)\subset{\mathbb{R}} with the Lebesgue measure σ\sigma.

The proposition above follows directly from the following theorem.

Theorem 3.13.

Let a<b∈ℝa<b\in{\mathbb{R}} and f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]. Assume that, there exists N>0N>0 such that ∫abfm​(z)​𝑑z=0\int_{a}^{b}f^{m}(z)\,dz=0 for any m≥Nm\geq N. Then f⁡(z)=0f(z)=0.

It seems that the theorem above is known but we failed to find any published proof in the literature. We did notice that Madhav V. Nori [N] has studied the problem above in a much more general setting. It is very possible that Theorem 3.13 will follow from some results obtained in [N].

Jean-Philippe Furter [FZ] informed the author that he and his colleague Changgui Zhang have got an analytic proof for Theorem 3.13, which is under preparation. Mitya Boyarchenko [B] also sent the author a sketch of his brilliant but unpublished proof. Surprisingly, Boyarchenko’s proof is purely algebraic and uses only some results from algebraic number theory such as Dirichlet’s theorem on arithmetic progressions, etc.

Next, we end this section with a connection of the one-variable case of Conjecture 3.2 with the so-called polynomial moment problem proposed by M. Briskin, J.-P. Francoise and Y. Yomdin in the series of papers [BFY1]-[BFY5]. The polynomial moment problem is mainly motivated by the center problem for the complex Abel equation. The problem was recently solved by F. Pakovich and M. Muzychuk [PM] (See the theorem below). For more details on the polynomial moment problem, see the references quoted above and also citations therein. The author is very grateful to Harm Derksen, Jean-Philippe Furter, Jeffrey C. Lagarias, Leonid Makar-Limanov, Lucy Moser-Jauslin for communications and suggestions on this connection, and also to Fedor Pakovich for communications on his joint work [PM] with Mikhail Muzychuk.

Recall that the polynomial moment problem is the following problem: given any polynomial f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and a≠b∈ℂa\neq b\in{\mathbb{C}}, find all polynomials q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] such that, for any m≥0m\geq 0,

(3.20) ∫abfm​(z)​q​(z)​𝑑z=0.\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f^{m}(z)q(z)dz=0.

The problem above was solved recently by the following theorem obtained by F. Pakovich and M. Muzychuk [PM].

Theorem 3.14.

((Pakovich and Muzychuk)) Let a≠b∈ℂa\neq b\in{\mathbb{C}} and f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]. A non-zero polynomial q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] satisfies Eq. ((3.20)) for any m≥0m\geq 0 iff there exist some polynomials Qj​(z)Q_{j}(z), fj​(z)f_{j}(z) and Wj​(z)W_{j}(z) (j∈J)(j\in J) such that

(1)(1) Wj​(a)=Wj​(b)W_{j}(a)=W_{j}(b) for any j∈Jj\in J;

(2)(2) q⁡(z)=∑j∈JQj′​(Wj​(z))​Wj′​(z)q(z)=\sum_{j\in J}Q_{j}^{\prime}(W_{j}(z))\,W_{j}^{\prime}(z);

(3)(3) f⁡(z)=fj​(Wj​(z))f(z)=f_{j}(W_{j}(z)) for any j∈Jj\in J.

Note that, with the same notation as in Pakovich and Muzychuk’s theorem above, if we choose a<ba<b, B=(a,b)⊂ℝB=(a,b)\subset\mathbb{R} and the measure d​σ=q⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=q(z)dz (ignoring the positivity requirement on the measure σ\sigma for a moment), then Pakovich and Muzychuk’s theorem above gives all polynomials f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] such that ∫Bfm​(z)​𝑑σ=0\int_{B}f^{m}(z)\,d\sigma=0 for any m≥0m\geq 0.

But, unfortunately, Pakovich and Muzychuk’s theorem requires the integral in Eq. (3.20) vanish when m=0m=0, i.e. ∫B𝑑σ=∫Bq⁡(z)​𝑑z=0\int_{B}d\sigma=\int_{B}q(z)dz=0. From this requirement, it is easy to see that d​σ=q⁡(z)​d​zd\sigma=q(z)dz can not be a positive measure on the interval B=(a,b)B=(a,b). For example, q⁡(z)q(z) can not be any nonzero polynomial with real coefficients such that q⁡(c)≥0q(c)\geq 0 for any c∈Bc\in B. Therefore, Pakovich and Muzychuk’s theorem can not be applied directly to approach Conjecture 3.2.

Nevertheless, it is still very interesting to see if some of the techniques (instead of the main theorem) in [PM] can somehow be applied to study Conjecture 3.2 for the cases when q⁡(z)q(z) are polynomials or analytic functions in one variable which are non-negative over some open intervals of the real line.

On the other hand, we see that Conjecture 3.2 also raises a new question on the polynomial moment problem, namely, what is the solution of the polynomial moment problem with the (slightly weaker) condition that the integrals in Eq. (3.20) vanish for any m≥1m\geq 1 but not necessarily for m=0m=0? We believe this question is also very interesting to investigate.

4. Some General Results on Mathieu Subspaces

Note that the Mathieu conjecture (Conjecture 1.2), the IC (Conjecture 1.4) and its generalizations (Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2) discussed in the previous sections are all about whether or not certain subspaces are Mathieu subspaces of their ambient commutative algebras. Furthermore, this is also the case for the well-known Jacobian conjecture and the Dixmier conjecture through their equivalences (See [Z3] for the discussions on these equivalences) to some special cases of the IC. Therefore, it is necessary and important to study Mathieu subspaces separately in a more general setting.

In this section, we give some examples of Mathieu subspaces from other sources and derive some general results on this newly introduced notion.

First, let us generalize the notion of Mathieu subspaces defined in Definition 1.1 to associative but not necessarily commutative algebras.

Definition 4.1.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be an associative algebra over a commutative ring RR and ℳ{\mathcal{M}} a RR-subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. We say that ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a left Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} if the following property holds: for any a,b∈𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}} with am∈ℳa^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1, there exists N≥1N\geq 1 ((depending on aa and bb)) such that b​am∈ℳba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥Nm\geq N.

We define right Mathieu subspaces and also (two-sided) Mathieu subspaces in the obvious ways.

It is easy to see that any left ideal is automatically a left Mathieu subspace. Similarly, this is also the case for right and two-sided ideals. Therefore, the notion of Mathieu subspaces can be viewed as a generalization of the notion of ideals even for noncommutative algebras. But, as we will see from examples to be discussed in this section, many Mathieu subspaces are not ideals. Actually they are not even closed under the product of the ambient algebras.

We start with the following noncommutative examples of Mathieu subspaces.

Example 4.2.

For any n≥1n\geq 1 and integral domain RR of characteristic zero, let 𝒜=Mn×n​(R){\mathcal{A}}=M_{n\times n}(R) be the algebra of n×nn\times n matrices with entries in RR and ℳ{\mathcal{M}} the subspace of trace-zero matrices.

Note that, for any A∈𝒜A\in{\mathcal{A}}, Am∈ℳA^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1 iff AA is nilpotent. Then, for any B∈𝒜B\in{\mathcal{A}}, we have B​Am=Am​B=0∈ℳBA^{m}=A^{m}B=0\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥nm\geq n. Therefore, ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a two-sided Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} but certainly can not be an ideal of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} unless n=1n=1.

Next, from additive valuations on polynomial algebras, we can get the following family of Mathieu subspaces of polynomial algebras.

Example 4.3.

For any n≥1n\geq 1 and any integral domain RR, let 𝒜=R⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}=R[z] be the polynomial algebra over RR in nn variables zz. For any linear functional ν:ℝn→ℝ\nu:{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}, we define an additive valuation ordν:𝒜→ℝ∪{+∞}\mbox{ord}_{\nu}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{+\infty\} by setting, ordν​(0):=+∞\mbox{ord}_{\nu}(0)\!:=+\infty and, for any 0≠f⁡(z)∈𝒜0\neq f(z)\in{\mathcal{A}},

(4.1) ordν​(f):=min⁡{ν⁡(α)|the coefficient of zα in f⁡(z) is not zero}.\displaystyle\mbox{ord}_{\nu}(f):=\min\{\nu(\alpha)\,|\,\mbox{the coefficient of $z^{\alpha}$ in $f(z)$ is not zero}\}.

For any c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}, let ℳc{\mathcal{M}}_{c} be the subspace of polynomials f∈𝒜f\in{\mathcal{A}} such that ordν​(f)≥c\mbox{ord}_{\nu}(f)\geq c.

Then it is easy to check that, for any c>0c>0, ℳc{\mathcal{M}}_{c} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} but not necessarily an ideal of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} if ordν​(f)<0\mbox{ord}_{\nu}(f)<0 for some f∈𝒜f\in{\mathcal{A}}.

More generally, we have the following family of examples from commutative rings (viewed as ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-algebras) with valuations.

Example 4.4.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be any commutative ring and ν\nu a real-valued ((additive)) valuation (([AM], [Mat])) of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, i.e. μ:𝒜→ℝ∪{+∞}\mu:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{+\infty\} such that, for any x,y∈𝒜x,y\in{\mathcal{A}}, we have

(4.2) ν⁡(x)\displaystyle\nu(x) =+∞​ iff ​x=0,\displaystyle=+\infty\mbox{ iff }x=0,
(4.3) ν⁡(x​y)\displaystyle\nu(xy) =ν⁡(x)+ν⁡(y),\displaystyle=\nu(x)+\nu(y),
(4.4) ν⁡(x+y)\displaystyle\nu(x+y) ≥min⁡{ν⁡(x),ν⁡(y)}.\displaystyle\geq\min\{\nu(x),\nu(y)\}.

For any c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}, let ℳc{\mathcal{M}}_{c} be the subspace of elements xx of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} with ν⁡(x)≥c\nu(x)\geq c. Then it is easy to check that, for any c>0c>0, ℳc{\mathcal{M}}_{c} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} but not necessarily an ideal of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

Similar as for ideals, we say a Mathieu subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of an algebra 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is proper if ℳ≠0{\mathcal{M}}\neq 0 and ℳ≠𝒜{\mathcal{M}}\neq{\mathcal{A}}. From the example above, we see that some fields may actually have some proper Mathieu subspaces. Also, unlike proper ideals, proper Mathieu subspaces may contain some invertible elements. But, as we will see below, proper left or right Mathieu subspaces can not contain the identity element of the ambient algebras.

Lemma 4.5.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be any algebra and ℳ{\mathcal{M}} a proper left or right Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. Then, 1∉ℳ1\not\in{\mathcal{M}}.

Proof:  Assume otherwise. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, 1m=1∈ℳ1^{m}=1\in{\mathcal{M}}. Then, for any b∈𝒜b\in{\mathcal{A}}, b=1m​b=b​1m∈ℳb=1^{m}b=b1^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} when m>>0m>>0. Hence, we have ℳ=𝒜{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{A}} which is a contradiction.  □\Box

The next proposition will give us more examples of Mathieu subspaces of polynomial algebras, which are not necessarily ideals.

Proposition 4.6.

Let KK be a field of any characteristic. For any finite subset S={u1,u2,…,uk}⊂KnS=\{u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{k}\}\subset K^{n} and σ={a1,a2,…,ak}⊂K×\sigma=\{a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{k}\}\subset K^{\times}, denote by ℳ⁡(σ){\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) the subspace of polynomials f⁡(z)∈K⁡[z]f(z)\in K[z] such that

(4.5) ∑i=1kai​f​(ui)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}f(u_{i})=0.

Then, ℳ⁡(σ){\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) is a Mathieu subspace of K⁡[z]K[z] iff, for any non-empty subset S′⊂SS^{\prime}\subset S,

(4.6) ∑u∈S′u≠0.\displaystyle\sum_{u\in S^{\prime}}u\neq 0.

Proof:  First, the (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of the proposition can be proved by similar arguments as in the proof of Proposition 3.11. So we skip it here.

To show the (⇒)(\Rightarrow) part, assume that there exists a non-empty S′⊂SS^{\prime}\subset S such that Eq. (4.6) holds.

Let f⁡(z)∈K⁡[z]f(z)\in K[z] such that

(4.7) f⁡(ui)={1 if ​ui∈S′0 if ​ui∉S′.\displaystyle f(u_{i})=\begin{cases}1&\mbox{ if }u_{i}\in S^{\prime}\\ 0&\mbox{ if }u_{i}\not\in S^{\prime}.\end{cases}

Note that, such a polynomial f⁡(z)f(z) always exists. For example, when n=1n=1 (the idea for n>1n>1 is similar), we may choose

f⁡(z)=∑u∈S′∏c∈S;c≠u(z−c)∏c∈S;c≠u(u−c)\displaystyle f(z)=\sum_{u\in S^{\prime}}\frac{\prod_{c\in S;c\neq u}(z-c)}{\prod_{c\in S;c\neq u}(u-c)}

For any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

∑i=1kai​fm​(ui)=∑i∈S′ai=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}f^{m}(u_{i})=\sum_{i\in S^{\prime}}a_{i}=0.

Therefore, we have that fm​(z)∈ℳ​(σ)f^{m}(z)\in{\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Now fix an uj∈S′u_{j}\in S^{\prime} and g⁡(z)∈K⁡[z]g(z)\in K[z] such that g⁡(uj)=1g(u_{j})=1 and g⁡(ui)=0g(u_{i})=0 for any 1≤i≠j≤k1\leq i\neq j\leq k. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

∑i=1kai​(fm​g)​(ui)=∑i=1kai​fm​(ui)​g​(ui)=aj​g​(uj)=aj≠0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}(f^{m}g)(u_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}f^{m}(u_{i})g(u_{i})=a_{j}g(u_{j})=a_{j}\neq 0.

Therefore, fm​g∉ℳ⁡(σ)f^{m}g\not\in{\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) for any m≥1m\geq 1. Hence ℳ⁡(σ){\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) is not a Mathieu subspace of K⁡[z]K[z].  □\Box

Remark 4.7.

Note that, when k=1k=1, ℳ⁡(σ){\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) in Proposition 3.11 is always an ideal of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z]. But if k>1k>1, ℳ⁡(σ){\mathcal{M}}(\sigma) in general is not an ideal. For example, for any k≥2k\geq 2, choose K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}}, ai=1a_{i}=1 and any distinct ui∈ℂu_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k).

For Laurent polynomial algebras ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z], by Duistermaat and van der Kallen’s theorem, Theorem 1.3, we see that the subspace of Laurent polynomials with no constant terms is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z]. Another example of Mathieu subspaces of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z] is given by the following theorem which was first conjectured in [Z2] and later was proved in [EWZ].

Theorem 4.8.

Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be the subspace of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z] of Laurent polynomials f⁡(z)f(z) with no holomorphic part, i.e. [zα]​f​(z)=0[z^{\alpha}]f(z)=0 for any α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. Then, ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z−1,z]{\mathbb{C}}[z^{-1},z].

Next we show that some properties of ideals are also shared by Mathieu subspaces.

Proposition 4.9.

Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ{\mathcal{B}} be any algebras over a commutative ring RR, and φ:𝒜→ℬ\varphi:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{B}} an RR-algebra homomorphism. Then,

(a)(a) for any left Mathieu subspaces ℳi{\mathcal{M}}_{i} (1≤i≤m)(1\leq i\leq m) of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, ∩1≤i≤mℳi\cap_{1\leq i\leq m}{\mathcal{M}}_{i} is also a left Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

(b)(b) for any left Mathieu subspace 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} of ℬ{\mathcal{B}}, φ−1​(𝒩)\varphi^{-1}({\mathcal{N}}) is also a left Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

Proof:  (a)(a) Set ℳ:=∩1≤i≤mℳi{\mathcal{M}}\!:=\cap_{1\leq i\leq m}{\mathcal{M}}_{i}. It is easy to see that ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is also a RR-subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.

Let a,b∈𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}} with am∈ℳa^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1. For any 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, let Ni∈ℕN_{i}\in{\mathbb{N}} such that b​am∈ℳiba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}}_{i} for any m≥Nim\geq N_{i}. Let N:=max⁡{Ni| 1≤i≤m}N\!:=\max\{N_{i}\,|\,1\leq i\leq m\}. Then, for any m≥Nm\geq N, we have b​am∈ℳiba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}}_{i} for any 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m. Hence b​am∈ℳba^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥Nm\geq N.

(b)(b) Again, it is easy to see that φ−1​(𝒩)\varphi^{-1}({\mathcal{N}}) is a RR-subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} since φ\varphi is an RR-algebra homomorphism.

Let a,b∈𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}} with am∈φ−1​(𝒩)a^{m}\in\varphi^{-1}({\mathcal{N}}) for any m≥1m\geq 1. Set x:=φ⁡(a)x\!:=\varphi(a) and y:=φ⁡(b)y\!:=\varphi(b). Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have xm=φm​(a)=φ⁡(am)∈𝒩x^{m}=\varphi^{m}(a)=\varphi(a^{m})\in{\mathcal{N}}. Since 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} is a left Mathieu subspace of ℬ{\mathcal{B}}, there exists N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} such that y​xm∈𝒩yx^{m}\in{\mathcal{N}} for any m≥Nm\geq N. But y​xm=φ⁡(b)​φm​(a)=φ⁡(b​am)yx^{m}=\varphi(b)\varphi^{m}(a)=\varphi(ba^{m}), so we have b​am∈φ−1​(𝒩)ba^{m}\in\varphi^{-1}({\mathcal{N}}) for any m≥Nm\geq N. Therefore, φ−1​(𝒩)\varphi^{-1}({\mathcal{N}}) is a left Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}.  □\Box

Remark 4.10.

From the proof above, it is easy to see that Proposition 4.9 also holds for right or two-sided Mathieu subspaces.

Proposition 4.11.

Let KK be any field with uncountably many elements and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} a commutative KK-algebra. Let z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},...,z_{n}) be nn free commutative variables. Then, for any Mathieu subspace ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, ℳ⁡[z]⊂𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{M}}[z]\subset{\mathcal{A}}[z] is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}[z].

Proof:  Note first that, by using induction on the number of free variables zz, it will be enough to show the proposition for the one-variable case. So we assume n=1n=1.

We use the contradiction method. Assume the proposition is false. Then there exist f⁡(z),g⁡(z)∈K⁡[z]f(z),g(z)\in K[z] with fm∈ℳ⁡[z]f^{m}\in{\mathcal{M}}[z] for any m≥1m\geq 1 but fk​(z)​g​(z)∉ℳ⁡[z]f^{k}(z)g(z)\not\in{\mathcal{M}}[z] for infinitely many positive integers kk. Let {mi∈ℕ}\{m_{i}\in{\mathbb{N}}\} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that fmi​g∉ℳ⁡[z]f^{m_{i}}g\not\in{\mathcal{M}}[z] for any i≥1i\geq 1.

Note that, for any h⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡[z]h(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}[z] of degree d:=deg⁡h⁡(z)≥0d\!:=\deg h(z)\geq 0 and h⁡(z)∉ℳ⁡[z]h(z)\not\in{\mathcal{M}}[z], by using the invertibility of the Vandermonde matrices, it is easy to check that there are at most dd distinct elements c∈K×c\in K^{\times} such that h⁡(c)∈ℳh(c)\in{\mathcal{M}}. Otherwise, all the coefficients of h⁡(z)h(z) would be in ℳ{\mathcal{M}} and h⁡(z)∈ℳ⁡[z]h(z)\in{\mathcal{M}}[z].

Therefore, for each fixed mim_{i}, there are only finitely many c∈Kc\in K such that fmi​(c)​g​(c)∈ℳf^{m_{i}}(c)g(c)\in{\mathcal{M}}. Since KK has uncountably many distinct elements, there exists b∈Kb\in K such that fmi​(b)​g​(b)∉ℳf^{m_{i}}(b)g(b)\not\in{\mathcal{M}} for all i≥1i\geq 1.

But, on the other hand, since fm​(z)∈ℳ​[z]f^{m}(z)\in{\mathcal{M}}[z] for any m≥1m\geq 1, all the coefficients of fm​(z)f^{m}(z) are in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Since ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a KK-subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, we have fm​(b)∈ℳf^{m}(b)\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1. Furthermore, since ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a Mathieu subspace of 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and f​(b)m=fm​(b)∈ℳf(b)^{m}=f^{m}(b)\in{\mathcal{M}} for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have fm​(b)​g​(b)∈ℳf^{m}(b)g(b)\in{\mathcal{M}} when m>>0m>>0. In particular, fmi​(b)​g​(b)∈ℳf^{m_{i}}(b)g(b)\in{\mathcal{M}} when i>>0i>>0. Hence we get a contradiction.  □\Box

Finally, one remark on the sums of Mathieu subspaces is as follows.

Note that, by Proposition 4.9, (a)(a), the intersection of any finitely many Mathieu subspaces is always a Mathieu subspace. Naturally, one may wonder if the sum of any finitely many Mathieu subspaces is also a Mathieu subspace. But this is not true in general.

Example 4.12.

Let 𝒜=ℂ⁡[z]{\mathcal{A}}={\mathbb{C}}[z] in one variable zz. Let ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ2{\mathcal{M}}_{2} be the one-dimensional subspace spaces of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] spanned by 1+z1+z and 1−z1-z, respectively. Then, it is easy to check that both ℳ1{\mathcal{M}}_{1} and ℳ2{\mathcal{M}}_{2} are Mathieu subspaces of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] and ℳ:=ℳ1+ℳ2=ℂ⋅1+ℂ⋅z{\mathcal{M}}\!:={\mathcal{M}}_{1}+{\mathcal{M}}_{2}={\mathbb{C}}\cdot 1+{\mathbb{C}}\cdot z. But, since 1∈ℳ1\in{\mathcal{M}} and ℳ≠ℂ⁡[z]{\mathcal{M}}\neq{\mathbb{C}}[z], by Lemma 4.5 ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is not a Mathieu subspace of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].
